newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow police say security being tightened.
newsitem.headline: Moscow police say security being tightened.

text.p: Russia's interior ministry on Thursday ordered street patrols to be reinforced in Moscow and security tightened at major buildings, one day after security chief Alexander Lebed was accused of plotting to seize power.

The measures were ordered by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov as part of a series to stiffen security across Russia because of intelligence reports that Chechen separatist rebels were planning guerrilla strikes against Russian targets.

Kulikov accused Lebed on Wednesday of plotting to create a special force in a bid to seize power and said Lebed had been offered the services of 1,500 Chechen rebels to help him. Lebed and the rebels have denied the accusations.
Interfax news agency said an extra 2,000 interior ministry troops were being drafted into the capital.

Valentin Koval, a spokesman for the Moscow branch of the interior ministry, said the special interior ministry units would reinforce police patrols and the length of patrol shifts would be extended from 10 hours to 12 hours.
He said police checks would be tightened at entrances to the capital, routine checks of cars and drivers' documents would be stepped up and security beefed up outside major buildings.
He did not say which buildings this included but they were likely to include railway stations, airports and underground stations.
Security had already been tightened in Moscow after the start of fighting in breakaway Chechnya in December 1994. Road checks are frequent on the edge of the city and some police carry weapons.

More than 30 people were hurt in two bomb explosions on trolleybuses in Moscow last July and four people were killed in a bomb blast on the Moscow underground last June. But police have found no evidence of a Chechen link.
